young.html: After the western Roman Empire ended, the eastern half went on, ruled from the great city of Constantinople. Today we often call it the Byzantine Empire, but its people called themselves Romans.

Gibbon's second half tells a thousand years of stories: the emperor Justinian, who collected Rome's laws and built the huge church of Hagia Sophia; the rise of Islam and of new empires; Charlemagne, crowned emperor in Rome in AD 800; the Crusades; and the Mongols.

At last, in AD 1453, the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople with huge cannons, and the last Roman emperor died defending the walls. Gibbon ends his book back in the city of Rome, among the ruins where he first had the idea.

full.html: Volume 38 holds the second half of Gibbon's history (chapters 41–71, published 1788). It is wider than its title: besides the eastern empire it covers the Persians, the Arabs, the Franks, the Normans, the Turks and the Mongols, and the city of Rome in the Middle Ages.

Justinian (527–565) and his general Belisarius reconquered North Africa and Italy for a time; he rebuilt Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; and his lawyers gathered centuries of Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis. Gibbon's chapter 44 on Roman law is still admired, and the Code became a foundation of the civil law of much of Europe.

Chapters 50–52 tell of Muhammad, the rise of Islam and the Arab conquests that within a century reached from Spain to Central Asia. For his time Gibbon wrote with unusual curiosity and some admiration, describing Islam's teaching of one God and its law, though his account reflects the European sources and attitudes of the 18th century. Later chapters treat Charlemagne's empire (800), the quarrels over icons, the Crusades (from 1096), the sack of Constantinople by crusaders in 1204, the Mongols and the rise of the Ottoman Turks.

Mehmed II besieged Constantinople in the spring of 1453 with an army and great cannons. The emperor Constantine XI fell in the final assault on May 29, and the city became the Ottoman capital. Gibbon narrates the siege at length; for him it marks the end of the Roman Empire that began with Augustus.

full.html: The last chapters return to the city of Rome in the Middle Ages, the popes, the republican dream of Cola di Rienzo and the slow ruin of its ancient buildings. Gibbon closes with the memory that began it all:

full.text: It was among the ruins of the Capitol that I first conceived the idea of a work which has amused and exercised near twenty years of my life, and which, however inadequate to my own wishes, I finally deliver to the curiosity and candor of the public.

full.author: Edward Gibbon

full.note: the final sentence, dated Lausanne, June 27, 1787

full.html: Gibbon's summary phrase. Near the end he says he has described "the triumph of barbarism and religion," a phrase that shows both his admiration for Rome and the Enlightenment views of his time, which many readers then and now dispute.

Thinking the Byzantine Empire was a different, non-Roman state. Its people called themselves Romans, kept Roman law and saw their emperors as successors of Augustus; the name "Byzantine" was given later.

deep.html: Gibbon had a low opinion of the eastern empire, which he saw as a long, sad decline. Modern historians of Byzantium give a much fuller picture of its art, scholarship, diplomacy and long survival, and of how it preserved Greek learning that later reached Renaissance Italy. Historians of Islam likewise draw on many sources Gibbon could not read. His sweep across many peoples, though, made him one of the first writers of what we might call world history.
